docs.title: Fayde
docs.text:
Fayde finds the stars in a FITS image, matches them against a star catalog, and returns a world coordinate system (WCS) solution with its measured accuracy. It runs from the command line and from Python on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

To solve your first image, follow these pages in order:

  1. Install Fayde.
  2. Choose and connect a star catalog.
  3. Solve a frame.

docs.title: Get the UCAC4 catalog
docs.text:
Fayde reads the UCAC4 catalog (Zacharias et al. 2013) from a local copy of its original binary files. Fayde doesn't include the catalog. The Strasbourg astronomical Data Center (CDS) publishes it as catalog I/322A. The download is about 8.9 GB.

To download the catalog, use a terminal on Linux or macOS, or PowerShell on Windows. In the download commands, use curl.exe in place of curl on Windows:

  1. On Linux or macOS, create the catalog directories:
mkdir -p UCAC4/u4b UCAC4/u4i

On Windows, create the directories:

mkdir UCAC4\u4b, UCAC4\u4i
  1. Go to the u4b directory:
cd UCAC4/u4b
  1. Download the 900 zone files, z001 to z900:
curl -fO "https://vizier.cfa.harvard.edu/ftp/cats/I/322A/UCAC4/u4b/z[001-900]"

If the download stops, start it again from the file that was downloading. For example, if it stopped at z412, change the range to z[412-900].

  1. Go to the u4i directory:
cd ../u4i
  1. Download the two index files:
curl -fO "https://vizier.cfa.harvard.edu/ftp/cats/I/322A/UCAC4/u4i/{u4index.unf,u4hpm.dat}"

Fayde uses u4index.unf to seek directly to the stars that it needs and u4hpm.dat for the proper motions of fast-moving stars. If u4index.unf is missing, Fayde finds the same stars by searching each zone file.

  1. Return to the directory where you started:
cd ../..
  1. On Linux or macOS, count the zone files:
ls UCAC4/u4b | wc -l

On Windows, count the zone files:

(Get-ChildItem UCAC4\u4b).Count

Check that the output is 900. If it's lower, download the missing files again.

The catalog directory has this layout:

UCAC4/
├── u4b/
│   ├── z001
│   ├── ...
│   └── z900
└── u4i/
    ├── u4hpm.dat
    └── u4index.unf

When a Fayde command has a --ucac4 option, give it the path to the UCAC4 directory, which is the directory that contains u4b. Download all 900 zone files, because Fayde reports an error when a zone that it needs is missing.

docs.title: Pattern indexes for sub-degree fields
docs.text:
A pattern index lets Fayde solve a frame when the pointing or pixel scale is uncertain or unknown. If you know the pointing and have a precise pixel scale from a frame header or instrument profile, you need only the UCAC4 catalog.

An index covers fields near its target field of view. Fayde chooses among the indexes you provide. To cover a wider range of scales, follow these steps:

  1. Build an index for each field of view.
  2. Pass each index to fayde solve with a separate --index option.

docs.title: Build the recommended indexes
docs.text:
The two recommended indexes cover the whole sky at epoch 2025.0. You need the full UCAC4 catalog, with all 900 zone files, and at least 32 GB of free memory.

Replace UCAC4_DIR with the path to the directory that contains u4b. To cover both field sizes, build both indexes:

  1. Build the index for fields of about 1°:
fayde index build --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --fov 1.0 --stars-per-fov 23.7 --pattern-stars-per-fov 23.7 --mag-limit 15.5 --min-edge 0.04 --epoch 2025 -o allsky-1.0.fidx
  1. Build the index for fields somewhat wider than 1°:
fayde index build --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --fov 1.3 --stars-per-fov 40 --pattern-stars-per-fov 20 --stars-per-field 12 --mag-limit 15.5 --min-edge 0.05 --epoch 2025 -o allsky-1.3.fidx

The builds used the version 0.1.0 binary on a 32-core x86_64 Linux computer. Other jobs ran on the computer during the builds, with a load of about 38. The table lists the build results:

Index Stars Patterns File size Build time Peak memory allsky-1.0.fidx 1,572,824 259,900,180 17,211,606,974 bytes 30 min 26 s 22.7 GB allsky-1.3.fidx 1,572,824 153,951,343 10,218,984,414 bytes 21 min 50 s 13.6 GB

docs.title: Plan for memory
docs.text:
Fayde loads the entire index into memory. On an otherwise idle 64-bit Arm computer, fayde index info loaded each recommended index with these results:

Index Load time Peak memory allsky-1.0.fidx 48 s 18.3 GB allsky-1.3.fidx 27 s 10.9 GB

The fayde command loads the index each time that it runs. To solve many frames, use the Python package and reuse one fayde.Solver, which loads the index once.

docs.title: Check a content hash
docs.text:
Each index has a content hash, a 64-bit checksum that covers its stars, patterns, and build options. Fayde uses the hash to identify the index that produced a solution and detect file damage. The hash isn't a cryptographic signature. Fayde records each index's hash in the identity.indexes[].content_hash field of the solve report.

To compare your index with the expected hash, follow these steps:

  1. Print the index metadata:
fayde index info allsky-1.0.fidx
  1. Compare the content_hash field in the output with the table below.

An index's bytes and hash don't depend on the platform or build profile. Fayde uses fayde_core::Portable for all its math. Builds from the full UCAC4 catalog with the commands on this page produce these hashes:

Index content_hash allsky-1.0.fidx 1ddf14fa50ad59dd allsky-1.3.fidx 4ad74722223054e1

Version 0.1.0 and every later version build the same bytes. If a release changes the bytes, the release notes describe the change, and this page lists the new hashes.

Continuous integration doesn't build the recommended indexes, because each one takes tens of gigabytes of memory and about half an hour.

docs.title: Index build options
docs.text:
To list every option and its default value, run fayde index build --help. The table describes the options used in the recommended commands:

Option Meaning --fov The field of view that the index is built for, in degrees --stars-per-fov The number of stars kept per field of view, selected uniformly over HEALPix cells --pattern-stars-per-fov The number of those stars, taken brightest first, that form patterns --stars-per-field The number of stars per lattice field from which patterns are formed --mag-limit The faintest magnitude considered --min-edge The shortest pattern edge, in degrees. Below it, centroid errors dominate --epoch The epoch that the star positions are propagated to, as a Julian year --region RA,DEC,RADIUS Builds a regional index, in degrees, instead of an all-sky index. A regional build takes minutes, which makes it useful for tests

For more information about the algorithms, see the references.

docs.title: Install Fayde
docs.text: Use pip install to install both the Python module and the fayde command. To use the command without Python, install the command-line tool on its own. Then get the UCAC4 catalog.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To install Fayde, use a computer that runs one of these systems:

  • Linux on x86_64 or 64-bit Arm, with glibc 2.17 or later
  • macOS 11 or later, on Apple silicon or an Intel processor
  • Windows 10 or later, on x86_64

You also need the following:

  • About 9 GB of free disk space for the UCAC4 catalog
  • For the Python package, CPython 3.10 or later

To solve a frame, you also need a FITS image from your own observation. The image must meet these requirements:

  • The stars are point sources, as in an image taken with sidereal tracking. Fayde doesn't yet detect trailed stars.
  • The image isn't compressed with fpack. To decompress an image, use the funpack program from CFITSIO.
  • The header gives the pointing and the pixel scale. If it doesn't, you can specify them yourself.

docs.title: Install the command-line tool
docs.text: Each release includes a prebuilt fayde binary. You don't need Rust to install it. After you install the tool, continue to Get the UCAC4 catalog.

docs.title: Install on Linux or macOS
docs.text:
To install the latest release, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, identify your operating system and processor architecture:
uname -sm
  1. Set the platform variable to the value that matches the output:
Output of uname -sm Value Linux x86_64 linux-x86_64 Linux aarch64 linux-aarch64 Darwin arm64 macos-arm64 Darwin x86_64 macos-x86_64

For example, for the output Darwin arm64, set the variable to macos-arm64:

platform=macos-arm64
  1. Download the archive:
curl -LO "https://github.com/shaneryall/Fayde/releases/latest/download/fayde-$platform.tar.gz"

Optional: Before you extract the archive, check it as described in Verify a download.

  1. Extract the archive:
tar -xzf "fayde-$platform.tar.gz"

Extraction creates a directory named fayde- followed by your platform value. The directory contains the fayde binary, the license files, and an example instrument profile.

  1. Install the binary in /usr/local/bin, which is on your PATH:
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/bin && sudo install -m 755 "fayde-$platform/fayde" /usr/local/bin/fayde

If sudo prompts for your password, enter it.

  1. If macOS blocks a binary that you downloaded with a web browser instead of curl, remove the quarantine attribute to allow it to run:
sudo xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /usr/local/bin/fayde
  1. Check the installation:
fayde --version

The output is similar to the following:

fayde 0.3.0 (0123456789ab)

docs.title: Install on Windows
docs.text:
To install the latest release, follow these steps:

  1. In PowerShell, download the archive:
curl.exe -LO https://github.com/shaneryall/Fayde/releases/latest/download/fayde-windows-x86_64.zip

Optional: Before you extract the archive, check it as described in Verify a download.

  1. Extract the archive:
Expand-Archive fayde-windows-x86_64.zip -DestinationPath .

Extraction creates a directory named fayde-windows-x86_64. The directory contains fayde.exe, the license files, and an example instrument profile.

  1. In the current PowerShell session, add the extracted directory to Path:
$env:Path += ";$PWD\fayde-windows-x86_64"

The Path change lasts until you close PowerShell.

  1. Check the installation:
fayde --version

The output is similar to the following:

fayde 0.3.0 (0123456789ab)

Optional: To keep the Path change after you close PowerShell, follow these steps:

  1. In the Windows search box, enter environment variables.
  2. Select Edit environment variables for your account.
  3. Select Path.
  4. Click Edit.
  5. Click New.
  6. Enter the full path of the extracted directory.
  7. Click OK.

docs.title: Verify a download
docs.text:
Each release includes a SHA256SUMS file that lists the SHA-256 checksum of every other file in the release.

To check an archive on Linux or macOS, follow these steps:

  1. In the directory that contains the archive, download the checksum file:
curl -LO https://github.com/shaneryall/Fayde/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS
  1. Compare the checksums. On Linux, use sha256sum:
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

On macOS, use shasum:

shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS

The output names the archive, followed by OK.

To check the archive on Windows, follow these steps:

  1. In PowerShell, in the directory that contains the archive, download the checksum file:
curl.exe -LO https://github.com/shaneryall/Fayde/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS
  1. Print the checksum of the archive:
(Get-FileHash fayde-windows-x86_64.zip -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
  1. Print the expected checksum:
Select-String fayde-windows-x86_64.zip SHA256SUMS
  1. Compare the checksums from the two outputs. The archive is intact when they match. Uppercase and lowercase letters are equivalent.

A checksum shows that the archive is intact. Releases from 0.3.3 on also have a build attestation, which shows that a GitHub Actions workflow of the Fayde repository built the archive. Optional: To check it, run this GitHub CLI command in the directory that contains the archive:

gh attestation verify ARCHIVE --repo shaneryall/Fayde

Replace ARCHIVE with the archive's filename, for example fayde-linux-x86_64.tar.gz. The command fails if no attestation from the Fayde repository matches the archive.

docs.title: Install with Cargo
docs.text:
You need Rust 1.85 or later to build the fayde command from crates.io. To build and install the command, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, install the fayde-cli crate:
cargo install --locked fayde-cli

Cargo installs fayde in its binary directory, which is ~/.cargo/bin unless you changed it. If your shell can't find fayde, add that directory to your PATH.

  1. Check the installation:
fayde --version

A build from crates.io shows unknown in place of the commit. The output is similar to the following:

fayde 0.3.0 (unknown)

docs.title: Install the Python package
docs.text:
The fayde package on PyPI includes a prebuilt wheel for every supported platform. Each wheel supports CPython 3.10 and every later version, and you don't need Rust to install it. The package installs both the Python module and the fayde command.

If PyPI has no wheel for your platform, pip builds the package from its source distribution. You need Rust 1.85 or later for that build.

To install the package, follow these steps:

  1. On Linux or macOS, in a terminal, create a virtual environment:
python3 -m venv .venv

On Debian and Ubuntu, this command needs the python3-venv package.

On Windows, in PowerShell, create the virtual environment:

py -m venv .venv
  1. On Linux or macOS, activate the virtual environment:
source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows, activate the virtual environment:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

If PowerShell reports that running scripts is disabled, follow these steps:

  1. Allow scripts for the current session:

    Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned

  2. Activate the environment again.

  3. Install the package:

python -m pip install fayde
  1. Check the installation:
python -c "import fayde; print(fayde.__version__)"

The output is the version number, for example 0.3.0.

  1. Check that you can run the fayde command:
fayde --version

The output is similar to the following:

fayde 0.3.0 (0123456789ab)

The command is available while the virtual environment is active.

To solve a frame from Python, see Use Fayde from Python.

docs.title: Use Fayde from Python
docs.text:
To install the package, see Install the Python package.

To open the catalog and load the indexes only once, reuse one solver for every frame. To find the stars in an image and solve it, create the solver and call solve_image:

import fayde

solver = fayde.Solver("/path/to/UCAC4")
report = solver.solve_image("frame.fits")
if report["solved"]:
    cards = report["wcs_cards"]

Replace /path/to/UCAC4 with the path to your catalog directory and frame.fits with the path to your FITS image.

The image argument accepts the path to a FITS file, a 2-D NumPy array, or an Astropy HDU. For an array, pass the frame's header with header. You can use Fayde without NumPy or Astropy.

If you detect the stars yourself, pass their positions to solve. In this example, x, y, and flux are sequences of the source positions and fluxes from your detector, and hdr is the image header. The indexes and instrument arguments are optional. To solve the source list, check the WCS, and find catalog stars at the source positions, use these methods:

solver = fayde.Solver("/path/to/UCAC4", indexes=["allsky-1.0.fidx"])
report = solver.solve(x, y, flux=flux, header=hdr, instrument="profiles/example.json",
                      deadline=5.0)
if report["solved"]:
    cards = report["wcs_cards"]
    check = solver.verify(x, y, cards, header=hdr)
    stars = solver.stars_at(cards, x, y, header=hdr)

To find the stars in an image without solving it, use fayde.detect:

detection = fayde.detect("frame.fits")
sources = detection["sources"]

The Python interface follows the command line:

  • The solve, solve_image, and verify methods take the command-line options under the same names with underscores, such as pointing_sigma and relax_priors_on_failure. In Python, run help(fayde) to list them. The detect and stars_at functions have their own options. To list those options, run help(fayde.detect) and help(fayde.Solver.stars_at).
  • Input coordinates x and y are 0-based unless you pass origin=1. Pixel fields in the report are 1-based, as in FITS and in the command-line report.
  • The header argument accepts a dictionary, a list of header cards, or an astropy.io.fits.Header.
  • The instrument argument accepts a profile dictionary or the path to a profile file.
  • The report is a dictionary with the same fields as the command-line JSON report.
  • An invalid option raises ValueError. A solver failure raises fayde.FaydeError, which stores the report in its report attribute.
  • Fayde releases the global interpreter lock (GIL) while it solves, so threads can share one Solver.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Every algorithm Fayde uses, where it comes from, and where it lives in the code. When an algorithm has no published source, the entry says so. Keep this file in step with the code: a change that adds or replaces an algorithm updates its entry here, and the implementing module's doc comment cites the same source.

Geosci. 42, 49 Pattern field centres crates/fayde-index/src/build.rs (lattice) 4-star patterns: sorted edge ratios, binned key, canonical order by distance from centroid Brown & Stubis 2017, "TETRA: Star identification with hash tables", AIAA/USU Conference on Small Satellites; tetra3 (ESA, github.com/esa/tetra3) Pattern shape and hash key; pattern-hash hypotheses in the solver crates/fayde-index/src/pattern.rs, crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_hash) Two-tier index (selection v4): dense verification stars plus greedy brightest-first pattern thinning (ties by ID), minimum separation r_min = 0.6 × fov / sqrt(N), N = pattern_stars_per_fov; pattern membership stored per star (file format v2) ESA tetra3 (generate_database, pattern/verification densities and separation rule); Brown & Stubis 2017 / TETRA About N pattern stars per fov² without coarse-cell brightness artifacts; achieved density depends on input density crates/fayde-index/src/build.rs (select_pattern_stars, pattern_min_sep, build_selected) Lattice fields with a fixed pattern budget, breadth-first brightest-first combinations, prime-sized table, linear probing, 16-bit key check, largest-edge prune, nearest-bin-first lookup cedar-solve (github.com/smroid/cedar-solve, fork of tetra3); no paper Index construction and lookup crates/fayde-index/src/build.rs, pattern.rs, lib.rs (lookup) Multiplicative hashing (constant 2654435761 ≈ 2³²/φ) and linear probing Knuth 1998, The Art of Computer Programming vol. 3, 2nd ed., §6.4 Pattern table addressing crates/fayde-index/src/pattern.rs k-d tree Bentley 1975, Commun. ACM 18(9), 509 Radius searches over star vectors crates/fayde-index/src/kdtree.rs Radius search on a uniform grid of cells (the cell method for fixed-radius near neighbours) Bentley & Friedman 1979, ACM Comput. Surv. 11(4), 397, a survey of range searching in which cells are one of the structures Matching sources to the reference stars of one hypothesis (the points change with every refit, so a structure filled in one pass beats one that is sorted) crates/fayde-solve/src/grid.rs Multiply-rotate hash for keys that are already numbers ("Fx hash") Firefox, and the Rust compiler's rustc-hash crate; no paper Hash maps keyed by grid cells and star identities, in place of SipHash crates/fayde-solve/src/hash.rs Bayesian log-odds verification (true star vs distractor mixture, unique reference claims, ranked sources) Lang et al. 2010, AJ 139, 1782, §2.4 Accepting or rejecting a hypothesis crates/fayde-solve/src/verify.rs Score = largest cumulative log-odds over prefixes of the ranked list; the stars a hypothesis was built from are matched but not scored astrometry.net solver/verify.c (keeps the best index; takes the quad's stars out of its lists), the bestlogodds loop, and the quad's stars moved out of the test list. The prefix maximum is the quantity Ville's maximal inequality bounds for a non-negative supermartingale: Ville 1939, Étude critique de la notion de collectif Source lists with many faint false detections; no evidence from matches that hold by construction crates/fayde-solve/src/verify.rs Pair-separation list with range lookup (k-vector idea; binary search instead of the k-vector's linear interpolation). The pairs are put in bins by squared chord length, and a bin's separations are worked out and sorted when a lookup first reaches it: a lookup returns what the fully sorted list would Mortari 1997, J. Astronaut. Sci. 45(2); Mortari & Neta 2000, AAS 00-128; the bins and the deferred sort are Fayde's Pair seeds for hinted solving crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (PairTable) Progressive sampling: seeds from the best-ranked sources first, ranking by p_star × flux Chum & Matas 2005, CVPR (PROSAC); the scale-prior ordering below is a Fayde extension Source ordering, seed order crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs Local optimization: re-match and refit each promising hypothesis before scoring Chum, Matas & Kittler 2003, DAGM, LNCS 2781 (LO-RANSAC) local_refit crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs Number of false alarms; threshold on log-odds − ln(hypotheses tested) Desolneux, Moisan & Morel 2000 (a-contrario); Moisan & Stival 2004, IJCV 57(3) Acceptance that does not loosen as the search grows crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs Similarity seeds from 2 or 4 correspondences: closed-form complex least squares, z_c = α z_p + β or α conj(z_p) + β, starting in the catalogue-centroid tangent plane and refitted with the tangent point at the fitted CRVAL (see Fayde's own choices) Planar equivalent of Umeyama 1991, IEEE TPAMI 13(4), 376–380 (least-squares similarity); related rotation fit: Kabsch 1976, Acta Cryst. A32, 922 Rotation, isotropic scale, translation and both parities without affine shear; also local refits with fewer than 8 matches crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (similarity_seed, rematch_fit) Cauchy IRLS weights 1 / (σ_tot² (1 + (r/r0)²)), source and catalogue variance added in quadrature Holland & Welsch 1977, Commun. Stat. 6(9); r0 = 3 σ_tot is Fayde's tuning choice Robust local refits before verification crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (local_refit) IRLS with mixture-model inlier probabilities as weights Holland & Welsch 1977, Commun. Stat. 6(9); Hogg, Bovy & Lang 2010, arXiv:1008.4686 Final WCS fit crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs, solve.rs (final_fit) Error-scale factor (reduced χ², Birge ratio) Birge 1932, Phys. Rev. 40, 207 Calibrates default centroid errors and detects under-reported producer errors; per-source floors are a Fayde choice below crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (final_fit) SIP distortion convention (A, B, AP, BP) Shupe et al. 2005, ASP Conf. Ser. 347, 491 Distortion model, FITS cards crates/fayde-wcs/src/sip.rs Distortion fit as a full polynomial in the tangent plane, decomposed into CD + SIP Lang et al. 2010 (astrometry.net tweak) Final fit at order ≥ 2 crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (fit_poly) Model order by BIC with noise variance profiled out: n·ln(χ²/n) + k·ln n, n = 2 Σ inlier_prob, k = 2 × polynomial terms Schwarz 1978, Ann. Stat. 6(2), 461; soft effective sample size is a Fayde choice Choosing TAN vs SIP order 2–3 independently of a common centroid-sigma rescaling crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (fit_best_order) Scale and roll priors as terms of the final fit: a Gaussian prior on a linear-model parameter as one more weighted observation Gelman et al. 2013, Bayesian Data Analysis 3rd ed., ch. 14 (prior information as additional data points); the linearisation along CD₀ and ∂CD₀/∂θ, leaving skew and anisotropy free, is Fayde's Holding sparse (5–15 star) fits near the instrument scale and roll crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (LinearPrior, solve_with_prior), solve.rs (linear_prior) Parameter covariance of weighted least squares, (AᵀWA)⁻¹ scaled by the reduced χ² Press et al. 2007, Numerical Recipes 3rd ed., §15.4 Solution::covariance, predicted position errors crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (WcsCovariance) Index series in scale bands (√2 field-size steps), best-matched band first Lang et al. 2010, AJ 139, 1782 Blind solving across unknown pixel scales crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (solve_with_indexes) FITS file structure, binary tables (TFORMn, big-endian), header-only WCS files Pence et al. 2010, A&A 524, A42 (FITS 3.0); IAU FITS Working Group 2016, FITS Standard 4.0 Reading source lists, images and headers, writing source lists and .wcs crates/fayde-fits/src/lib.rs, sources.rs, image.rs Source-list format (frame.sources.fits): a FITS binary table with X/Y in FITS pixels, optional FLUX, SIGMA/SIGMA_PX, P_STAR, TRUNCATED, and IMAGEW/IMAGEH Fayde's own (docs/source-list.md). The X/Y columns and IMAGEW/IMAGEH match the tables astrometry.net reads and writes (Lang et al. 2010), so those files read unchanged Input from any detector; output of fayde detect crates/fayde-fits/src/sources.rs Civil date → day number Hinnant, "chrono-compatible low-level date algorithms" (2013, howardhinnant.github.io/date_algorithms.html) DATE-OBS → MJD crates/fayde-fits/src/priors.rs (mjd_from_iso) FNV-1a 64-bit hash Fowler, Noll & Vo; Noll, Vo, Eastlake & Hansen 2026, RFC 9923 Index content hash for provenance and corruption checks crates/fayde-index/src/file.rs

docs.title: Fayde's own choices (no published source)
docs.text: Choice Rationale Code Incremental Cartesian unit-vector buckets of side at least the separation chord, searching 27 neighbouring buckets and checking exact distances Bounded local searches for streaming insertion/replacement and pattern thinning, without rebuilding the static k-d tree; independent of HEALPix boundaries crates/fayde-index/src/build.rs (SeparationGrid) High-proper-motion cut: drop a star from patterns if |μ| × 25 yr > 0.5 × pattern_max_error × fov/2 A shift δ changes ratios by ≈ δ / (largest edge); keeps motion-induced ratio error within half a bin over the index lifetime crates/fayde-index/src/build.rs Default proper-motion error 50 mas/yr where UCAC4 has none Value UCAC4 itself uses for "no data" in output tables (readme note 9) crates/fayde-catalog/src/ucac4.rs Strict-by-default catalogue queries (missing zone = error) An empty cone must never be mistaken for empty sky crates/fayde-catalog/src/lib.rs Pre-filter: ≥ 2 of the next 12 ranked sources must land on seed-list catalogue stars within 3σ + 2 px + 1% of distance from the seed pair Tolerance grows with distance because a 2-star seed's rotation/scale error does crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (prefilter) Reference count per hypothesis: brightest clamp(round(1.5 × Σ p_star), 10, 2000) catalogue stars in the frame, using usable sources after duplicate demotion (p_star defaults to 1) Effective real-source count prevents low-probability detections from inflating background density; placeholder until detection_limit is supported (design doc §6.2) crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs Local-refit radii 12 → 6 → 3 px; similarity fit below 8 matches, affine from 8 Tuned on synthetic fields; four to seven stars cannot constrain shear and anisotropy crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (local_refit, rematch_fit) A polynomial order above 1 is a BIC candidate only with four observations per parameter, n ≥ 4k (24 matches for order 2, 40 for order 3); n ≥ 2k while a tune-up is still collecting matches, whose result is refitted under the strict rule The profiled BIC has no floor: as k approaches n the fit interpolates, χ² → 0 and n·ln(χ²/n) → −∞. Measured without a rule, hinted solves of sparse frames: 43 of 60 frames with 6 stars and 52 of 60 with 10 stars returned a WCS wrong by ≥ 15″ at the corners. Short of interpolation it stays too liberal with outliers among a few dozen matches: on 1,200 undistorted frames of 12–50 stars, n ≥ 2k chose distortion 16 times (corner errors up to 107″), n ≥ 3k 5 times, n ≥ 4k once (3″); a BIC margin of up to 50 instead of a count still left 3 crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (fit_best_order) Similarity fits are repeated with the tangent point moved to the fitted CRVAL until it stops moving A transform found in another point's tangent plane is rotated by (east offset × tan δ) at CRVAL (convergence of the meridians). Measured: median hypotheses per hinted solve at Dec 86–89° fell from 607 to 6, the same as at low declination crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (similarity_seed) Distortion tune-up: a hypothesis that is not conclusive under a linear model, or that matches over 1.25× (+3) as many stars at 12 px as inside its own gates, is re-matched at 12 px with the order chosen by BIC until no more stars join, then at 6 and 3 px; the better-scoring of the linear and tuned models is kept, and the tune-up counts as one more hypothesis Fayde's own. With lens distortion a linear model leaves the outer stars outside the match gate. astrometry.net also refits a promising match before deciding (tune-up in solver.c, recalled from the source), without distortion. Measured: 5% distortion with 0.3 px centroids went from 18/30 solved (4 of them wrong by > 3″) to 30/30, none wrong crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (tune, try_hypothesis) A distortion polynomial is kept only if its confident matches cover the sources: in a 3 × 3 grid, every cell with ≥ 6 sources must have a matched fraction ≥ 0.25 × the frame's overall matched fraction; otherwise TAN, or no solution if the hypothesis only passed with distortion A polynomial locked onto part of the frame was wrong by up to 80 px in the rest (10% distortion test). Good fits had a lowest cell ratio of 0.47, partial locks ≤ 0.13 crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (covers_sources, final_fit) The fitted WCS must itself clear the acceptance threshold; the final IRLS runs until the match set and error scale repeat (at most 20 iterations, at least 4) The returned solution should be the one that passed, at a converged fit crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (final_fit) SIP inverse AP/BP of order forward + 2, fitted on a 25×25 grid; Fayde itself inverts by fixed-point iteration on A/B (exact to 1e-10 px) A quartic leaves 0.03 px at the corners of a cubic barrel; order + 2 gives < 0.01 px for external FITS readers crates/fayde-wcs/src/sip.rs Settle the match set with two TAN iterations before letting BIC consider SIP Avoids fitting distortion to a match set chosen by a wrong model crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (final_fit) A distortion order is kept only if no lower order predicts held-out cells of the frame (3 × 3, each left out in turn, training sets at n ≥ 2k) within 5% of its squared error; the lowest such order is used. Matches in fewer than 4 cells allow no distortion; when the order itself cannot be scored, BIC's order stands Spatial block cross-validation: Roberts et al. 2017, Ecography 40, 913. On simulated undistorted frames whose matches carry errors in one region, BIC took order 3 and the polynomial ran up to 146 px off in the corners crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs (held_out_order), crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (supported_order) When the request has a scale or roll prior, a final fit that ends with distortion is converged again as TAN with scale and roll free of the priors, matching afresh. Both are scored on the same sources at the distortion fit's error scale. A TAN outside the hint's hard limits replaces the distortion fit if it explains the sources at least as well (the hard limits then refuse it); a TAN inside them replaces it only with higher posterior odds, priors included Fayde's own. With the hint's scale wrong by more than its limits, the scale stopped inside them and distortion made up the rest with partly wrong matches (42.7 px off in the corners, log-odds 394); a trailed frame with smear did the same (30.7 px). With both checks the first gives no solution and the second solves to 0.03 px; of 106 simulated frames solved with distortion, 8 more are correct and none worse; 178 of 186 real-frame solutions stay bit-identical and the other 8 move closer to the Gaia references crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (converge) Header priors order: XPIXSZ/FOCALLEN, then a unit-checked linear WCS (CD, or PC × CDELT), then PIXSCALE/SECPIX; headers with both CD and PC give no scale; pointing from CRVAL then RA/DEC then OBJCTRA/OBJCTDEC; time from JD-OBS, MJD-OBS, then DATE-OBS (+TIME-OBS), all + EXPTIME/2 for mid-exposure No published source; CUNIT = 'degree(s)' accepted alongside FITS deg because some real headers use it crates/fayde-fits/src/priors.rs Tangent-plane inverse defined for every input: beyond 1e150 rad the reference-point term is dropped and only the direction of the offset is kept (the limit of the gnomonic inverse, 90° from the reference point); a NaN offset gives the reference point A WCS or pixel at the edge of the f64 range gave a panic; the limit is the mathematically defined answer crates/fayde-wcs/src/tan.rs (Basis::deproject) Header numbers must be finite: NaN, inf and exponents past the f64 range are kept as text, so a numeric read of that keyword is an error naming it A non-finite WCS or SIP value must not reach the arithmetic, and must not be read as an absent term crates/fayde-wcs/src/header.rs (parse_value), crates/fayde-wcs/src/sip.rs Repeated keyword: the first card is the one looked up Matches the lookup of cfitsio and Astropy, so a header that repeats a keyword gives the same WCS in each crates/fayde-wcs/src/header.rs (Header::get) Plausible epoch range, Julian years 1800 to 2200: a header clock outside it is reported and skipped, a request or index epoch outside it is an error A Julian Date in MJD-OBS or an unset camera clock otherwise moves every star by centuries of proper motion and fails with an unrelated message crates/fayde-core/src/epoch.rs, crates/fayde-fits/src/priors.rs, crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (validate) Header pointing is used only when the header does not declare another frame: RADESYS other than ICRS or FK5, or EQUINOX other than 2000, drops it with a warning (a bare EPOCH is not consulted: it is also written for the observation date); right ascension outside [0°, 360°) or 24 h is rejected, not wrapped No precession is applied, so B1950 or equinox-of-date coordinates are up to about 0.7° from ICRS; a prior must not be those coordinates read as ICRS crates/fayde-fits/src/priors.rs (foreign_frame, header_priors) Blind hypotheses whose implied frame exceeds twice the index field size are skipped before any catalogue query An index cannot hold patterns larger than its fields; such hypotheses produced sky-sized cones (found in a comparison run on real frames) crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_hash) Catalogue cones cached per (HEALPix cell of the field centre, √2 field-radius bucket) Avoids one catalogue query per blind hypothesis crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_hash) Catalogue stars of a pointing prior read as hypotheses need them: only the brightest stars of the prior's cone for seeding (Catalog::cone_brightest), and every star in a cone of 1.25 × the frame's radius around a hypothesis that passes the pre-filter; after 6 such reads the rest of the prior's cone is read in one go A 2° prior around a 0.6° frame covers 46 frame areas, and reading, propagating and sorting all of it was three quarters of a hinted solve. A hypothesis sees the stars it would see with the whole cone in memory, in the same order: results on 109 real frames are unchanged to the last bit. Of those solves, 62 needed one read and 1 the whole cone crates/fayde-solve/src/refset.rs, solve.rs (pair_seeds, prior_cone) Cone test that computes the exact separation only at the edge: a star whose J2000 direction is farther from the centre than the radius plus the largest proper motion is rejected on a dot product; the others are decided by the chord from the vector the propagation produced, and centre.separation(position) > radius is evaluated only within 1e-9 rad of the edge (and for cones wider than 1 rad) The exact form costs two sines, two cosines and an arctangent per star on top of the propagation. Compared with a record-by-record scan: 1.7 million stars in 720 cones equal, including 5,565 cones whose edge passes through or beside a star crates/fayde-catalog/src/ucac4.rs (ConeTest) Pair seeds within 3σ of the pointing before the whole prior cone, when 3σ is at most half the hard radius A pointing is usually known far better than the limit set on it, and the work of a pair-seed stage grows with its cone's area. 3σ holds 98.9% of a two-dimensional Gaussian. The first look is skipped when it would be more than half the limit (the default σ is a quarter of it): it would then cost nearly as much as the search it spares, and a frame it cannot solve would pay twice. Measured on 146 real source lists: 8.7 ms per list at a 2° limit, 1.1 ms at 0.25° crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (plan, pair_seeds) Instrument profile from solved frames (fayde calibrate): median fitted scale, with 1σ = 1.5 × its robust spread and at least 0.1% of the scale; parity when every solution agrees; roll rule offset + sign × keyword for the sign whose offsets scatter less, offset the median about the mean direction, 1σ = 2 × the robust spread (at least 0.05°), hard limit 10σ (at least 1°); pointing 1σ = median offset between the header pointing and the solved frame centre, divided by √(2 ln 2) Medians and median absolute deviations, so that poor solutions among the frames do not move the profile. The 0.1% floor: the solver's hard limit is 3σ on the scale fitted to one frame, and fits to a dozen stars scatter by 0.1 to 0.2% (a σ of 0.0013″ on 2.994″ lost a frame). √(2 ln 2) is the median of a Rayleigh distribution in units of its σ: the radial offset of a pointing with a Gaussian error σ per axis. A profile needs no other solver: 66 cold solutions gave 2.99361″/px and roll = 90.015° − keyword, scatter 0.039° crates/fayde-api/src/calibrate.rs Header read without its WCS (--no-header-wcs, profile header_wcs: false): the cards of a world coordinate system are dropped before the priors are read, so the pointing comes from RA/DEC or OBJCTRA/OBJCTDEC and no scale from CD or CDELT A header WCS may be another plate solver's solution, which a test of Fayde alone must not use and which later frames may not have crates/fayde-wcs/src/header.rs (without_wcs), crates/fayde-api/src/lib.rs (build_request) Cone search without u4index.unf: binary search of each zone file by RA; the records it leads to are checked for RA order A catalogue copy without u4i/ read whole zones: 350 ms per hinted solve, where a copy with the index took 22 ms. The search reads the records the index gives (see the UCAC4 entry above) crates/fayde-catalog/src/ucac4.rs (ra_range) Pattern search depth: top 16 ranked sources, breadth-first Dense synthetic fields abstained with 10 (all-sky benchmark); breadth-first order keeps the cost on frames the smaller depth could not solve crates/fayde-solve/src/request.rs (Policy::pattern_sources) Adaptive search plan from request metadata (pair seeds / ringed region hash / scale-pruned hash / blind / opt-in out-of-prior), shared hypothesis count across stages Fayde's own crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (plan, solve_auto) Region filter: all 4 pattern stars within (ring radius + implied field radius) of the pointing Rejects off-region hash matches before any fitting crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_hash) Placeholder scale rejection: a scale implying a field wider than a hemisphere (solver) or than 60° half-diagonal (header reader) Found on cropped frames whose headers carry non-WCS scale values crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (new_ctx), crates/fayde-fits/src/priors.rs Prior terms in the hypothesis score: ln(prior density / uniform density over the hard limits) for pointing (2-D Gaussian vs a cap of the hard radius), scale and roll (1-D Gaussians vs their ranges) Standard Bayesian odds (the same framework as Lang et al. 2010's verification); the uniform-over-limits reference is Fayde's choice crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (prior_log_ratio) Catalogue position error at epoch added in quadrature to the centroid error, per match Standard error propagation; uses Star::pos_err_mas from §5.1 crates/fayde-solve/src/verify.rs, solve.rs Duplicates: a source within 3 px of a better-ranked one gets p_star × 0.1 and is ranked last Detector fragments otherwise compete for the same reference star crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (new_ctx) Ranking: measured-flux sources by p_star × flux, then sources without flux in input order One missing flux must not discard all flux information crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (new_ctx) Polynomial fits in normalized offsets (u/S, v/S), coefficients rescaled by S^-(p+q) Standard least-squares conditioning (Press et al. 2007, §15.4); a safeguard: tests at 4096 px, orders 3 and 5, matched with and without it crates/fayde-solve/src/fit.rs, crates/fayde-wcs/src/sip.rs Leave-one-out residuals r/(1 − h) with leverage h = w·fᵀ(AᵀWA)⁻¹f; worst predicted σ over a 5×5 grid Hoaglin & Welsch 1978, Am. Stat. 32(1), 17 (the hat matrix); the grid report is Fayde's crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (final_fit), fit.rs (worst_radial_sigma_arcsec) Truncated sources: anisotropic Gaussian gate along the frame trail (1σ = L/2), excluded from fits and seeds Fayde's own crates/fayde-solve/src/verify.rs, solve.rs Instrument profile with a header-keyword roll rule Fayde's own crates/fayde-fits/src/instrument.rs, profiles/example.json verify_wcs / refine_wcs (fayde verify, fayde refit): score an existing WCS; re-match 12 → 6 → 3 px and refit with the solver's IRLS/BIC Fayde's own, reusing Lang et al. 2010 verification crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs Strategy: pair seeds first when there is a pointing prior and σ/scale ≤ 3%, then the pattern hash; the hash alone otherwise (including no priors) Follows the design (§5.3) and the oversampling measurement in §5.2 crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (solve_with_index) Pattern-hash ratio tolerance clamp(8.5σ / L, 0.002, 0.02), L = largest image edge Propagated centroid noise (≈ 2√2σ/L per ratio) × 3 crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_hash) Pattern-hash assignments: enumerate all ≤ 24 image permutations whose six labelled edge ratios (each divided by the largest edge) agree within lookup tolerance; fit both similarity parities, retain radial RMS ≤ 3 × max source σ, try smallest RMS first; require ≥ 1 extra index-star hit Canonical centroid-distance ranks can swap under noise; the similarity fit is sourced above, while enumeration, thresholds and residual ordering are Fayde choices crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pattern_seeds, pattern_hash) Hypothesis count starts after hard priors pass; each surviving permutation/parity is a separate trial, including cheap pre-filter failures Hard-prior rejections lie outside the searched model space; retains the NFA penalty for every eligible tested seed crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pair_seeds, pattern_hash) Catalogue pair traversal starts nearest the separation implied by the scale-prior mean, then alternates outward on either side Fayde's prior-guided extension of PROSAC (Chum & Matas 2005); tries plausible scales before the low edge of the permitted interval crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (pairs_from_mean) Default centroid sigma may shrink under the fitted error scale; producer-supplied sigma retains a floor of 1 on its multiplier A policy default is an initial estimate; measured producer errors remain a lower bound, including mixed source lists crates/fayde-solve/src/solve.rs (final_fit), verify.rs (assess) Detection pipeline as a whole: the star width measured from the frame and the filter matched to it (binning wide stars), one closed-form fit per peak supplying position, error, size and shape, classes and probabilities passed on to the solver's verification No detector surveyed (docs/research/literature-review.md §7) adapts its filter to a measured width, reports a per-star position error, or traces streaks before solving crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs; docs/design/detection.md Position error of the maximum of a filtered image, σx = σt² / (√2·σk·SNR); photon-noise term σp²·σt⁸ / (N·σk⁴·(σk² + 2σp²)²) Derived (docs/design/detection.md §4): noise gradient over signal curvature. Equal to the Cramér–Rao bound and to Mortensen et al.'s eq. 6 for a matched kernel; on synthetic frames the error over the claim has a robust spread of 0.8 to 1.25 crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (finish) Star width as the widest distinct mode of the size distribution of bright, round peaks (histogram of ln size, bins of 0.25; a mode needs 5% of the tallest and a dip to half below it) Nothing from the sky is sharper than the optics, and stars share one width where hot pixels and cosmic rays have many. A real frame from a warm detector had 300 radiation hits to 36 stars; a median took the hits' width and the frame did not solve crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (measure_psf) Star shape: the frame's narrow-axis variance and axis ratio, medians over the peaks of the star mode; "sharp" is under 0.4 of the narrow-axis variance, "extended" and streak seeds are 1.5 and 2 times the stars' own axis ratio A drift during the exposure smears every star alike. Judged against the mean width, the 36 brightest stars of a real frame smeared two to one were classed as cosmic rays, and the frame did not solve crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (measure_shape, classify), streak.rs Local test: a peak must stand above the median of a ring at three star-widths by the threshold less one σ, where the ring disagrees with the mesh A mesh cannot follow stray light or halos. Synthetic glow of 20 × sky from a corner: 33 false stars without, 1 with crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (stand_out), peaks.rs (ring_median) Mesh tiles replaced only when above the largest of the four two-neighbour line means; straight-line extrapolation of the background beyond the outermost tile centres A 3 × 3 median flattens the corner of a frame lit from outside, and a mesh held flat to the edge turns a gradient into signal (111 false sources at the edge of a binned frame before, 3 after) crates/fayde-detect/src/mesh.rs (despike, at) Detection threshold as min(pixel tail, peak density) for a number of noise peaks per frame (default 1) A maximum above u on pixels is a pixel above u, so the pixel count bounds the continuous-field density where that overshoots (narrow kernels). Counted on empty frames: within 45% for σk 0.7 to 2 px crates/fayde-detect/src/stats.rs Classes and their limits: sharp under 0.4 of the stars' variance; extended over 2 × or elongated over 1.5, each beyond 2.5 × the fit's error 2/SNR; class factors on p_star of 0.9 (saturated) and 0.5 (extended) Tuned on synthetic frames. The error of a fitted minor-axis variance was measured at 0.9 to 1.6 /SNR of the total with a bias of −1.3/SNR crates/fayde-detect/src/lib.rs (classify) Saturation level from flat-topped peaks at the frame's brightest level; centre of a saturated star from the core of its saturated region (pixels with long runs along both axes); error 0.1 px + 3% of the core radius A bleed trail has short runs across it; a flat top below the brightest level is a cosmic-ray track or a stuck column. Measured: centre within 0.6 px for stars 3 to 300 × saturation with trails crates/fayde-detect/src/saturate.rs, lib.rs (find_saturation) Streak tracing: seeds from ridge-like peaks (elongation ≥ 2), a walk along a running least-squares line (search ± 2 px, threshold 3σ, gaps of 8 px + 10% of the points, at most 30), end clean-up, total-least-squares line, half-level ends, a second trace from the fitted line, acceptance (10 px and 8σ long, half covered, SNR 10, half of the bright peaks ridges), cosmic_ray when narrower than 0.4 of the stars' variance Fayde's own; a line model through the walk keeps it on course across a crossing streak. Measured: ends within 2 px, 0.2 px typical crates/fayde-detect/src/streak.rs

docs.title: Considered and not adopted
docs.text: Algorithm Source Why not A pattern-hash stage ahead of the pair seeds when a pointing, a tight scale and an index are all given Fayde's own Measured on 146 real source lists of 4 to 60 sources with the two all-sky indexes. The hash stage solved 123 of the 134 solvable lists and halved the median (1.3 ms against 2.8 ms), but a stage that finds nothing costs 37 to 395 ms in a 17 GB table (1 ms in a regional one, which is what first suggested the idea), and a match that comes late costs up to 86 ms: mean 24.0 ms against 4.5 ms with the pair seeds first. A cap on the stage gains under 10%. Pair seeds solved every list the hash did Radon-transform streak search (fast Radon transform; median Radon) Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018, AJ 156, 229; Stark et al. 2022, ACS ISR 2022-08 Finds long streaks below the per-pixel noise, at about 0.9 to 10 s per megapixel after stars are removed. Fayde needs streaks kept out of the star list, which only streaks above the threshold threaten. Hough transform on thresholded pixels (kernel-based: Fernandes & Oliveira 2008; Rubin maskStreaks) Pattern Recognition 41, 299; DMTN-197 Each ridge-like peak already carries its direction, so a trace from it replaces the vote. A-contrario alignment of points Lezama et al. 2015, IEEE TPAMI 37(3), 499 For grouping fragments of a faint streak; the tracer follows the pixels instead. Its significance test would suit a fragment-only detector. Exact null distribution of peak heights with Benjamini–Hochberg selection (STEM) Schwartzman, Gavrilov & Adler 2011, Ann. Stat. 39, 3290; Cheng & Schwartzman 2017 The continuous-field formula is 25 to 35% conservative for a kernel of about 1 px (Lin, Schwartzman & Davenport 2025, arXiv:2501.13239); the pixel bound is tighter there and is used with it. Iterative Gaussian-windowed centroid Bertin & Arnouts 1996 (SExtractor XWIN) Equal accuracy on the matched-filtered peak at a fraction of the cost. 4-D quad codes searched in a kd-tree Lang et al. 2010 Fayde's 5 sorted edge ratios describe the same four-point shape as a quad code, and the hash lookup already enumerates neighbouring bins and re-checks the exact shape, which is the continuous-tolerance behaviour a kd-tree gives. What astrometry.net adds for blind solving is its scale-band index series, which Fayde adopts.

docs.title: Source list format
docs.text:
A source list contains the positions of sources that you detect in one image. Use a source list when you detect the stars yourself. When you give Fayde the image with --image, you don't need a source list.

Fayde reads a source list with the --sources option of fayde solve, fayde verify, and fayde refit. The fayde detect command writes one with -o.

docs.title: File structure
docs.text:
A source list is a FITS file with a binary table extension. Each row of the table describes one source. Fayde reads the first binary table that has X and Y columns and ignores columns that this page doesn't list. Fayde recognizes a source list by this table, not by the filename.

Name a source list after its image, with the suffix .sources.fits. For example, use frame.sources.fits for the source list from frame.fits.

The fayde detect command sets the table's EXTNAME keyword to SOURCES and records the Fayde version in the CREATOR keyword. Fayde doesn't require these keywords in a source list that you write yourself.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
The following table lists the columns that Fayde reads:

Column Required Content X Yes The horizontal position of the source, in pixels Y Yes The vertical position of the source, in pixels FLUX No The integrated flux, in any linear unit. Fayde uses it to order the sources by brightness SIGMA or SIGMA_PX No The 1σ centroid error, in pixels. Fayde ignores a value that isn't positive P_STAR No The prior probability that the source is a real star, from 0 to 1. Fayde ignores a value outside that range TRUNCATED No Whether the frame edge or a mask cuts the source. A logical or integer column, where a nonzero value means true

Positions follow the FITS pixel convention: the center of the first pixel is at (1, 1), and X increases along a row of the image.

When a source has no SIGMA value, Fayde uses the value of --pixel-error, which is 1 pixel by default.

docs.title: Image size
docs.text: Fayde needs the width and height of the image. In the table header or the primary header, set the IMAGEW and IMAGEH keywords to the dimensions in pixels. If the source list doesn't have these keywords, Fayde takes the size from the frame header (--header) or from the --width and --height options.

docs.title: Write a source list
docs.text:
In this example, x, y, and flux are sequences with one value for each source, and the image is 4,096 by 4,096 pixels. To write and solve a source list, follow these steps:

  1. In Python, with the astropy package installed, write the source list with an Astropy table:
from astropy.table import Table

table = Table({"X": x, "Y": y, "FLUX": flux})
table.meta["IMAGEW"] = 4096
table.meta["IMAGEH"] = 4096
table.write("frame.sources.fits", format="fits")
  1. In a terminal, solve the source list with --sources:
fayde solve --sources frame.sources.fits --header FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • FRAME: The path to the FITS image
  • UCAC4_DIR: The path to the directory that contains u4b
  • OUTPUT: The path to the WCS file to write

For more information about solving a frame, see Solve a frame.

docs.title: Use the command line
docs.text: To install the fayde command, see Install Fayde. To download the catalog for solving, see Get the UCAC4 catalog.

docs.title: Solve a frame
docs.text:
To solve an image with the local catalog and check the result, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, pass the FITS image and the catalog to fayde solve:
fayde solve --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • FRAME: The path to the FITS image, for example frame.fits
  • UCAC4_DIR: The path to the directory that contains u4b
  • OUTPUT: The path to the WCS file to write, for example frame.wcs

The directory of OUTPUT must exist, and OUTPUT can't be one of the input files. If a path contains spaces, enclose it in quotation marks.

Fayde finds the stars in the image and reads the pointing, pixel scale, observation time, and image size from its header. Fayde then prints a JSON report to standard output.

  1. Check the report's solved field:

  2. When solved is true, Fayde writes the solution to OUTPUT as FITS WCS header cards.

  3. When solved is false, Fayde writes no solution, and the report's reason field says why.

Fayde returns an exit status of 0 when the run completes, with or without a solution. If the run fails, Fayde returns an exit status of 1 and prints the error to standard error.

When a run writes no solution, Fayde removes any file that already exists at OUTPUT. Fayde keeps the file if it rejects the command before the run starts, if it can't write to OUTPUT, or if OUTPUT is one of the input files.

docs.title: Use your own source list
docs.text:
If you detect the stars yourself, pass a source list with --sources in place of the image. A source list is a FITS binary table with X and Y columns. For the columns that Fayde reads, see the source list format.

To solve a source list, pass it together with the FITS file that has the frame's header:

fayde solve --sources SOURCES --header FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace SOURCES with the path to the source list, for example frame.sources.fits. Fayde uses only the header from the file at FRAME.

docs.title: Detect stars without solving
docs.text:
To find the stars in an image and write them as a source list, use fayde detect:

fayde detect --image FRAME -o SOURCES

Fayde prints a JSON report with the background, the noise, the width of the stars, and every source that it found. The report also lists the streaks that cross the image, such as satellite trails, and the hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits that Fayde set aside. With -o, Fayde also writes the sources to SOURCES, in the format that --sources reads.

When the stars' full width at half maximum (FWHM) is about one pixel or less at full resolution, Fayde keeps point sources that are too sharp for the usual shape checks. A star this narrow can put nearly all its light in one pixel, so the source list can also include hot pixels and compact cosmic-ray hits.

If background subtraction clipped many sky pixels to the same minimum value, such as zero, Fayde accounts for the clipping when estimating the background and setting the detection threshold. The clipped-sky model requires floor pixels mixed with sky noise across most of the image's sky tiles. Frames with a constant border and ordinary sky use the standard background estimate.

To list the detection options and their default values, run fayde detect --help. The same options work with fayde solve --image. The --detect-threshold option sets the peak threshold in σ of the filtered image, and its value must be at least 1.5.

docs.title: Specify the pointing and scale
docs.text:
Command-line values take precedence over the instrument profile, which takes precedence over the frame header. To solve an image whose header lacks the pointing or the pixel scale, specify them:

fayde solve --image FRAME --ra RA --dec DEC --scale SCALE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace the following:

  • RA and DEC: The right ascension and declination of the image center in degrees
  • SCALE: The pixel scale in arcseconds per pixel

When you solve a source list without a frame header, Fayde also needs the image size. Add --width and --height, in pixels, unless the source list has the IMAGEW and IMAGEH keywords.

To decide whether you need these options, check the frame header. Fayde reads keywords such as the following:

Information Header keywords Pointing CRVAL1 and CRVAL2 of a header WCS, RA and DEC, or OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC Pixel scale XPIXSZ with FOCALLEN, the CD matrix, CDELT1 and CDELT2, PIXSCALE, or SECPIX Observation time JD-OBS, MJD-OBS, or DATE-OBS, with EXPTIME or EXPOSURE Image size NAXIS1 and NAXIS2

If the header has no observation time, Fayde uses the epoch 2000. To set the epoch, use --epoch.

Fayde searches within 2° of the pointing. To change the limit, use --radius. To specify the pointing accuracy, use --pointing-sigma with the 1-sigma error in degrees. When that error is at most a sixth of the limit and the pixel scale is known to within 3%, Fayde first searches within 3 sigma of the pointing. It widens the search to the limit only when it finds no solution there.

To ignore the pointing and pixel scale from a WCS in the frame header, for example a WCS that another plate solver wrote, add --no-header-wcs. Fayde then reads the header pointing only from RA and DEC, or from OBJCTRA and OBJCTDEC.

To list every option and its default value, run fayde solve --help.

docs.title: Use an instrument profile
docs.text:
An instrument profile is a JSON file with settings that frames from one instrument share: the pixel scale, parity, a rule for deriving the roll from a header keyword, and the pointing accuracy in the frame headers. To use a profile, add --instrument:

fayde solve --image FRAME --instrument PROFILE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o OUTPUT

Replace PROFILE with the path to the profile file.

The repository contains an example profile, profiles/example.json. A release archive has the same file in the extracted archive's profiles directory. The example's values are illustrative. To create a profile for your instrument, follow these steps:

  1. Copy profiles/example.json.
  2. Edit the copy with your instrument's values. The source field of the example explains the scale and roll values.

If you don't know your instrument's values, use Fayde to measure them from its solved frames.

docs.title: Calibrate an instrument profile
docs.text:
You don't need another plate solver to calibrate a profile. For the initial solves, you need the pointing in the frame headers and an approximate pixel scale. To create a profile from these solutions, follow these steps:

  1. In a terminal, solve at least five frames with an approximate pixel scale:
fayde solve --image FRAME --scale SCALE --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR -o WCS

Replace the following:

  • SCALE: The pixel scale in arcseconds per pixel, correct to within 5%
  • WCS: The path to the WCS file to write, for example frame.wcs. Use a different path for each frame.

For each frame whose report has solved set to true, Fayde writes the solution to WCS. More frames give a better profile.

  1. List only the frames whose report has solved set to true in a text file, with one frame per line. Each line contains the path to the FITS image, a tab character, and the path to its WCS file, in that order.

  2. In a terminal, create the profile from the list with fayde calibrate:

fayde calibrate --solved LIST --roll-keyword ROLL_KEYWORD --binning XBINNING,YBINNING -o PROFILE

Replace the following:

  • LIST: The path to the text file from the previous step
  • ROLL_KEYWORD: The header keyword that holds the instrument's roll angle in degrees
  • PROFILE: The path to the profile to write, for example camera.json

If the headers have no roll keyword, omit --roll-keyword. If the headers don't record the binning in XBINNING and YBINNING, omit --binning or name the keywords that they use.

Fayde prints the profile and writes it to PROFILE.

A calibrated profile has the following fields:

Field Meaning scale_arcsec, scale_sigma_arcsec The median pixel scale of the solutions and its 1-sigma uncertainty, in arcseconds per pixel. With --binning, this is the scale of an unbinned frame. parity The parity of the solutions. Fayde omits this field when the solutions disagree. roll With --roll-keyword, the rule that gives the roll from the roll keyword, with its 1-sigma error and hard limit in degrees binning With --binning, the binning keywords that you named pointing_sigma_deg The 1-sigma error of the pointing in the headers, in degrees. Fayde omits this field when fewer than five headers have a pointing. calibration The numbers behind these values: frames used, spreads, and largest deviations

You can add two optional fields manually. The pointing_radius_deg field sets the search limit around the pointing in degrees, in place of --radius. The header_wcs field, when set to false, has the same effect as --no-header-wcs on every frame. To include header_wcs in the profile during calibration, add --no-header-wcs to the fayde calibrate command.

docs.title: Solve without a pointing or scale
docs.text:
When you know the pointing and have a precise pixel scale, Fayde needs only the catalog. In that case, omit --index. Fayde searches a pattern index only if it finds no solution around the pointing. This extra search delays the report when a frame has no solution. When the pointing or scale is uncertain or unknown, Fayde also needs a pattern index, which you build once from the catalog. To build the recommended indexes, see the index guide.

To solve with a pattern index and ignore all priors, use --index and --no-priors:

fayde solve --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --index INDEX --no-priors -o OUTPUT

Replace INDEX with the path to a pattern index, for example allsky-1.0.fidx. To use several indexes, add --index once for each file.

docs.title: Limit the search time
docs.text:
Search time increases with the area within the pointing radius. The following measurements show exhausted searches on a 32-core x86_64 Linux computer. The frames had a pixel scale of 3 arcseconds per pixel, a scale uncertainty of 0.1%, and unconstrained roll:

Pointing radius Hypotheses until exhausted Time 0.5° 250–760 0.01–0.02 s 1° 830–2,500 0.02–0.05 s 2° 2,900–10,500 0.07–0.16 s 4° 11,000–40,000 0.24–0.62 s 8° 47,000–157,000 0.9–2.3 s

Frames with hundreds of sources took more than 18 s at an 8° radius. To limit a search, use these options:

  • Use --max-hypotheses to limit the work independently of the computer's speed.
  • Use --deadline to limit wall-clock time from the start of the request.

Each search stage in the report ends with an outcome: solved, exhausted, deadline, or hypothesis limit. When Fayde finds no solution, the report names the stage that a limit stopped. A search with a 1° radius takes about 50 times less work than one with an 8° radius.

docs.title: Check or refit an existing WCS
docs.text:
Replace WCS with the path to the WCS file to check, for example frame.wcs. OUTPUT must be a different file from WCS.

To check a WCS from any solver against the catalog, use fayde verify:

fayde verify --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS

To fit the WCS again from the matched stars and write the result, use fayde refit:

fayde refit --image FRAME --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS -o OUTPUT

Both commands also accept a source list: use --sources SOURCES --header FRAME in place of --image FRAME.

docs.title: Find catalog stars at a position
docs.text:
To find catalog stars at positions under a given WCS, use fayde verify. Specify pixel positions with --at, sky positions with --at-sky, or a source list with --at-sources.

To check positions from a source list, use --at-sources:

fayde verify --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS --header FRAME --at-sources SOURCES

To check a pixel position and a sky position at a specified epoch, use --at and --at-sky:

fayde verify --ucac4 UCAC4_DIR --wcs WCS --epoch 2020.89 --at 412.3,88.1 --at-sky 172.5,1.6

For each position, the report lists the following:

  • The nearest stars at the observation epoch and their separations
  • The combined 1σ uncertainty of the position, catalog, and WCS (--wcs-sigma)
  • The probability of an offset this large or larger if the position is the star (p_consistent)
  • The probability that some star lies this close to an arbitrary position (p_chance)

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: Fayde follows semantic versioning. While the version is 0.x, a breaking change increases the minor number, and anything else increases the patch number.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
The following changes are breaking:

  • Removing a command-line or Python option, or changing its meaning
  • Removing or renaming a JSON report field
  • Changing the index file format or the bytes of an index, including its content_hash

Adding a report field isn't a breaking change. If a release changes indexes, you must rebuild your indexes as directed in the release notes.

A fix that leaves reports and indexes unchanged is a patch release. So is a new command, option, or report field that changes nothing that already exists.

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text:
Before Fayde removes or renames a command-line option, a Python argument, or a report field, one release deprecates it:

  1. The release that deprecates it still accepts the old name and behaves as before. Fayde prints a warning that names the replacement, and the release notes list the deprecation.
  2. A later breaking release removes it, no earlier than the next minor version.

A change that can't keep the old behavior, such as a new index format, can't be deprecated first. Its release notes say what to do, for example to rebuild your indexes.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: Each release has a section in the changelog that lists its changes and marks the breaking ones. The same version is published on GitHub, PyPI, and crates.io.

docs.title: Star and streak detection — design
docs.text: Crate fayde-detect. Survey of existing methods: docs/research/literature-review.md §7. Sources of every algorithm: docs/references.md.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
Input: one image whose stars are points (a frame tracked at the sidereal rate, or a spacecraft holding its attitude), with possibly a satellite streak or two, hot pixels, cosmic-ray hits, saturated stars, stray light. Output: what the solver's input contract asks of a source list (plate-solver.md §6.3), filled honestly:

Per source How it is obtained x, y Closed-form fit to the peak of the matched-filtered image (§3.4) sigma_px Noise theory of that estimator, per source (§4) flux Integral of the fitted Gaussian p_star Local false discovery rate × shape class (§3.8) truncated The fit window reaches the frame edge

Streaks are traced and reported (ends, angle, width, flux), and every detection on one is kept out of the star list. Frames whose stars are trailed (tracking a satellite) are out of scope: their star list still comes from the host's own detector, as before.

Design targets, in order: no parameter the user must know (star width, noise and threshold are measured or derived; gain is read from the header when it is there); robust to cosmic rays by the hundred and to stray light; position errors that the solver's verification and fit can trust; speed; and the same bits on every machine (fayde_core::Portable, no platform maths).

docs.title: 2. Why not an existing detector
docs.text:
From the survey (literature review §7), what is in use today:

  • None measures the star width and adapts its filter. astrometry.net's simplexy smooths with a fixed σ = 1 px; DAOFIND and photutils need the FWHM from the user; SExtractor a fixed 3 × 3 kernel; cedar-detect a fixed 7-pixel gate with manual binning.
  • None reports a per-star position error to the matcher.
  • None runs a streak detector before solving. Streak fragments are rejected only as a side effect of size or shape gates, and astrometry.net removes only horizontal and vertical lines.
  • Hot pixels and cosmic rays are handled by minimum-area or sharpness heuristics that conflict with undersampled stars.
  • Licences: SExtractor GPL, SEP LGPL, astrometry.net GPL as distributed, cedar-detect source-available but not open source. Everything here is written from the papers, so no other project's code, and none of its licence terms, enters Fayde.

docs.title: 3. Method
docs.text:
image
  │ 1. matched filter (Gaussian; width measured, image binned if stars are wide)
  │ 2. background and noise mesh of the filtered image
  │ 3. peaks: local maxima above the false-alarm threshold
  │ 4. one closed-form fit per peak → position, size, shape, amplitude
  │ 5. local test: each peak against the ring around it
  │ 6. classes: star, saturated, extended, sharp
  │ 7. streaks: traced from ridge-like peaks
  │ 8. probabilities and errors
  ▼
stars (x, y, σ, flux, p_star) + streaks

docs.title: 3.1 Matched filter and scale
docs.text: The image is convolved with a Gaussian of the stars' width, the filter of highest signal-to-noise ratio for a point source in white noise. The width is not asked for. A first pass at σk = 1.2 px (within 7% of the best ratio for stars of FWHM 1.9 to 4.1 px) measures it (§3.3); a second pass is run only when the ratio 2·σk·σp / (σk² + σp²) falls below 0.93. Stars wider than σ = 2 px are binned first (block means), so wide-star frames cost less than narrow-star ones. At most three passes.

docs.title: 3.2 Background and noise
docs.text:
Tiles of 64 px (the same sky area on a binned image, down to 24 binned px), measured on the filtered image so that the noise is that of the thresholded quantity whatever the input's noise correlation.

  • Background: median of a sample of the tile, clipped once at median + 3σ.
  • Noise: 1.4826 × MAD / √2 of the differences of pixel pairs separated by more than the kernel's reach, clipped up to three times. A difference cancels the background and its gradient, which a spread of values would count as noise.
  • A tile standing above what its neighbours predict (a bright star, a galaxy) is replaced by the prediction: the largest, over the four lines through the tile, of the mean of its two neighbours on that line. SExtractor's 3 × 3 median flattens the corner of a frame lit from outside; this filter does not (the glow of stray light curves up along the direction to its source and down across it, and the line nearest that direction predicts at least the tile).
  • Between tile centres the values are bilinear; beyond the outermost centres the background is extrapolated in a straight line, so a gradient running off the frame is followed to the edge.

Clipped sky. If at least a quarter of the valid raw pixels equal the frame minimum, Fayde checks the distribution of those pixels in each tile. A tile is padding if at least 99% of its valid pixels equal the floor, or if transitions between floor and above-floor pixels occur at most a quarter as often as in a random mix. The detector checks the transition rate in tiles with at least eight floor pixels.

Fayde uses the clipped-sky model when more than half of the sky tiles with at least 24 valid pixels yield a fit. To fit a tile, at least a quarter of its valid pixels must be at the floor and at least 16 must be above it. The singly left-censored normal fit uses the floor fraction and an empirical quantile near the middle of the surviving values. Tiles without a fit use the frame's typical fit. When the model applies, floor pixels in padding tiles are undefined for detection. Otherwise, Fayde uses the standard filtered mesh.

The fit estimates the sky before clipping. Its clipped moments give the background and noise of the recorded pixels. Fayde propagates these through the point filter and accounts for the skew of the filtered noise when setting the peak threshold. On a simulated frame of 100 stars with 90% of the sky clipped at zero, 95 of 579 detections were stars before; with the model, 100 of 100, and every star is found. On 35 real frames with 25–36% of their pixels at zero, every frame still solves and the fit residual fell on 31 of them (median 0.40 to 0.35 px).

docs.title: 3.3 Star width
docs.text:
For a peak of the filtered image, the variance of the star's profile is the fitted variance (§3.4) less the kernel's. The frame's star width is taken from bright, round peaks, but they are not all stars: on a warm or irradiated detector hot pixels and cosmic-ray hits outnumber stars ten to one or more. Nothing that came through the optics is sharper than the optics allow, and stars share one width where artefacts have many. So the stars are the widest distinct mode of the size distribution: in a histogram of ln(size), the widest local maximum holding at least 5% of the tallest one's count and separated from narrower sizes by a dip to half its height. Blends and galaxies form a tail, not a mode.

The stars' shape is measured with their width: the median narrow-axis variance and the median axis ratio of the peaks in that mode. A drift during the exposure smears every star alike. Each source's narrow axis is then well under the stars' mean width, so narrowness (§3.6) and elongation (§3.6, §3.7) are judged against what the frame's stars show, not against a round star of the mean width.

docs.title: 3.4 One fit per peak
docs.text:
A quadratic surface is fitted by least squares to the logarithm of the 3 × 3 filtered pixels around the maximum. For an elliptical Gaussian this is exact, and it gives at once:

  • the position (no pixel-phase bias, unlike a quadratic fitted to the values themselves, whose bias reaches 0.03 px for these widths);
  • the variances along both axes and the orientation (eigen-decomposition of the fitted Hessian H: variance along an axis = −1/eigenvalue);
  • the amplitude, and so the flux 2π·A·σmajor·σminor.

Cost: nine logarithms and about 40 multiplications per peak.

docs.title: 3.5 Local test
docs.text: The mesh follows the frame on the scale of its tiles. Stray light and halos change faster, and what the mesh misses is left as broad bumps. A star is narrow: three widths from its centre nothing of it is left, so its height above the median of a ring of that radius (eight samples, robust to a neighbour or a streak crossing the ring) is its height; a bump two or more star-widths across falls short. Where the ring agrees with the mesh, the mesh (less noisy) stands; elsewhere the ring is the background and the peak must exceed it by the threshold less one σ. Saturated stars are exempt.

docs.title: 3.6 Classes
docs.text:
Class Test Goes to the solver sharp Narrowest axis under 0.4 of the stars' narrow-axis variance, beyond the fit's noise; or, in the unfiltered pixels, the second faintest of the four neighbours of the brightest pixel under half of exp(−1/σ²) of it (light through the optics reaches all four; charge deposited in the detector does not) no saturated Top at the saturation level (given, from the header, or the level of flat tops at the frame's brightest) yes, p × 0.9 extended Elongated over 1.5 times the stars' own axis ratio, or over twice the stars' variance, beyond the fit's noise yes, p × 0.5 streak On a traced streak no star The rest yes

A saturated star's centre is the mean position of the core of its saturated region: the pixels whose runs of saturated pixels along the row and along the column are each at least half the longest. A bleed trail, a few pixels wide, has short runs across it and does not move the centre. A saturated region that is a line of even width is a streak, not a star.

The work is bounded whatever the frame and the settings: each saturated pixel is flooded once per frame, a region is followed for at most 200,000 pixels, a saturation level within 20σ of the background is ignored, at most 200,000 peaks are measured and 1,000 streaks traced, and binning never leaves an image under 16 pixels on a side.

docs.title: 3.7 Streaks
docs.text:
A peak on a streak is a ridge: the fitted surface curves down across the streak and hardly at all along it. Each ridge-like peak (axis ratio at least twice the stars') seeds a trace: the ridge is followed one pixel at a time in both directions along a straight line refitted by least squares as points are added, re-centring on the brightest of five samples across the track, bridging gaps in proportion to the length traced. Holding the trace to a line keeps it on course past a bright star beside the streak or another streak crossing it. Then:

  • isolated points at the ends, short groups beyond a gap, and a bright star touching an end are removed;
  • the line is a total-least-squares fit; each end is put where the ridge falls to half its level (the true end of a uniform streak blurred by the PSF);
  • the streak is traced once more from the middle of the fitted line, whose direction is better than the seed's;
  • it is kept if it is at least 10 px and 8 cross-section σ long, half covered, with a total signal-to-noise ratio of 10, and if at least half of the bright peaks on it are ridges (a row of stars is not a streak);
  • a streak narrower than the stars is flagged cosmic_ray.

Only streaks bright enough to raise a peak above the detection threshold are found (about 5σ per PSF area). Fainter ones do not disturb the star list. Fayde does not search for them: an integration along the line (Radon transform; Nir, Zackay & Ofek 2018) costs 10 to 100 times everything here.

docs.title: 3.8 Threshold and probabilities
docs.text:
The threshold is set from the number of noise peaks the caller accepts per frame (default 1): the expected number of local maxima of filtered noise above u per pixel is bounded by min(P(Z > u), u·φ(u) / (4π·σk²)), the pixel count and the peak density of a continuous Gaussian field. On empty synthetic frames the bound is within 45% of the count for σk from 0.7 to 2 px. For a 4-megapixel frame the threshold is 5.0σ.

p_star = (1 − local false discovery rate) × class factor. The local rate is the expected number of noise peaks within a quarter σ of a source's height over the number of sources seen there. A source at the threshold in an empty region of height gets a low probability; the same height among many real faint stars gets a high one.

docs.title: 4. Position error
docs.text:
